intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself with the questions, and write your own notes in the space beside mine.

sections.title: What 'Post-Truth' Means
sections.big_idea: 'Post' means **facts no longer settle the argument.** They still exist, and emotion and belonging do the deciding.
in_plain_words: Oxford Dictionaries named post-truth its 2016 Word of the Year, after Brexit and the US election. The definition says objective facts are less influential than appeals to emotion and personal belief. It makes no claim that facts have vanished or that people are ignorant. It describes a condition of the public debate and says nothing about anyone's character.

Two ideas carry the section. In an old contest both sides accepted the same evidence and being caught wrong carried a cost. In a post-truth contest a claim is judged by which side it flatters, and exposure can even raise your standing. The infrastructure behind this is new: phones, feeds, group chats and an economy that pays for attention, while verification still costs a person's time.

diagram.caption: each era made reaching a million people cheaper

key_terms.meaning: Facts are less influential than emotion and personal belief in shaping opinion.
RAND's name for four symptoms, none of which needs an outright lie.
A source both sides trust to settle a factual dispute.
Producing falsehood became free while verifying a claim still costs a person's time.

worked_example.title: Which kind of contest?
worked_example.setup: Three illustrative situations. Label each as an old contest or a post-truth contest.
steps: Use the table: ask what settles it, what being caught costs, who referees, and how a correction lands.
Case 1: a minister is caught in a false claim and her own supporters cheer. Exposure raised her standing, so this is post-truth.
Case 2: an editor retracts a wrong figure after a court record is produced, and the paper loses readers. The cost is real, so this is the old contest.
Case 3: a fact-check is read by one camp as an attack by the other team. A correction taken as an attack is post-truth.
worked_example.answer: Cases 1 and 3 are post-truth; case 2 is the old contest. The cost of being caught is the quickest test.

mistakes: Reading 'post-truth' as 'facts have vanished'. The word means facts no longer settle the argument.
Blaming one platform or one party. The definition describes a condition of the public debate.
Using 'post-truth' to dismiss an opponent. A word that works as an insult stops working as a diagnosis.
Answering with a bigger pile of facts. The shared referee is rebuilt by being right when it was inconvenient.

recall.q: What did Oxford Dictionaries do in 2016?
recall.a: Named post-truth its Word of the Year, reporting a roughly twenty-fold spike in usage.

recall.q: Which row of the old versus post-truth table is the load-bearing one?
recall.a: The cost of being caught wrong.

recall.q: What are the four symptoms of truth decay?
recall.a: Disagreement about facts, blurred opinion and fact, rising volume of opinion over reporting, and declining trust in sources.

recall.q: What asymmetry explains the problem?
recall.a: Production got free; verification did not.

recall.q: Name two conditions that raise the stakes in South Asia.
recall.a: Any two of: mobile-first users, closed messaging, many languages, dense kinship networks, existing fault lines.

sections.title: A Taxonomy of Falsehood
sections.big_idea: Two questions sort the field: **is it false, and was harm intended?** The answer tells you whether to educate, debunk or defend.
in_plain_words: 'Fake news' is a poor working term. It lumps an honest mistake with a paid influence operation, says nothing about intent, and has become an insult for reporting someone dislikes. Misinformation is false and shared in good faith. Disinformation is false and spread to deceive. Malinformation is mostly true and used to wound.

The category belongs to the actor and the moment, so you cannot sort a message by reading it alone. In a chain of forwards, disinformation becomes misinformation when it reaches someone who believes it. That person is a target and not an author. Satire, rumour, hoax, clickbait and conspiracy theory fill out the family, and each needs a different response.

diagram.root: Is it false, and was harm intended?
diagram.caption: the two questions that sort every message

key_terms.meaning: False or misleading, spread without intent to deceive.
False, and created or spread deliberately to deceive or harm.
Accurate or private information used to cause harm.
Cues that marked content for one audience vanish when it travels to another.
An all-explaining secret-plot story that treats contrary evidence as proof.

worked_example.title: Sort three messages
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's own three cases and choose the response for each.
steps: An aunt forwards a false cure she believes. It is false with no intent to harm, so misinformation.
The same text, written by someone selling the cure. It is false and knowingly so, so disinformation.
A real leaked medical record posted to shame someone. It is true and used to harm, so malinformation.
Choose the response: correct privately and credit the motive; expose the operation and who gains; challenge the framing and protect the person targeted.
worked_example.answer: Misinformation, disinformation, malinformation. The first two share the same words, so the actor decides the category.

mistakes: Classifying a message by its text alone. The same words can be misinformation or disinformation depending on the sender.
Answering a worried relative as though they ran an influence operation. It loses the only channel you had.
Fact-checking a coordinated campaign claim by claim, which is the response it is designed to absorb.
Demanding the removal of misread satire. Restore the source and context instead.

recall.q: Which two axes separate mis-, dis- and mal-information?
recall.a: Whether the content is false and whether harm is intended.

recall.q: Who proposed the framework, and in which year?
recall.a: Wardle and Derakhshan, for the Council of Europe, in 2017.

recall.q: What is the most useful question for spotting an engineered campaign?
recall.a: Who gains if this is believed, and who gains if it is merely doubted?

recall.q: Why does malinformation defeat claim-by-claim fact-checking?
recall.a: Every claim is true, so the deception lives in selection and framing.

recall.q: What fast action reduces rumour after an incident?
recall.a: Say something true and specific early, even if it is only what you know and when you will know more.

sections.title: How Falsehoods Spread
sections.big_idea: False news travels farther, faster and deeper than true news, and **people, more than bots, do the spreading.**
in_plain_words: A study of about 126,000 stories on Twitter found that false news reached more people and went deeper into networks. False stories were more novel and set off surprise and disgust. Treat it as strong evidence for a real asymmetry, with limits: one platform, one period, stories rated by fact-checkers.

A rumour moves through four stages: seed, boost, cascade and saturate. The best chance to intervene is the boost stage, when a few high-reach accounts share it, yet most institutions respond at saturation. Closed chats, bots and coordinated networks add speed or a false impression of numbers. A forward from a relative carries the relationship's credibility, which no platform label can match.

diagram.caption: intervene at boost; by saturate only prebunking remains

key_terms.meaning: The stage where each share exposes new networks and corrections chase a moving front.
An automated account that amplifies to fake popularity or consensus.
Coordinated inauthentic behaviour: accounts working together while misleading about who they are.
Raised odds that you adopt a view because many others appear to hold it.
A cap on how many chats a message can be relayed to, slowing viral spread.

worked_example.title: How fast a forward multiplies
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures. One person forwards a rumour to 3 people, and each of them forwards it to 3 new people.
steps: Hop 1: 1 × 3 = 3 people reached.
Hop 2: 3 × 3 = 9 people reached.
Hop 3: 9 × 3 = 27 people reached.
Hop 4: 27 × 3 = 81 people reached.
worked_example.answer: 81 people by hop 4, from a single forward. Hubs such as large groups would make it faster still.

mistakes: Taking 'I keep seeing it' as confirmation. In a network where everyone forwards to everyone, it tells you about the network.
Aiming only at bots. The study found people did most of the spreading.
Quoting the 2018 finding as a universal constant. It covers one platform, one period and fact-checker ratings.
Accusing an account of being a bot on opinion alone. Ask for evidence of coordination.

recall.q: What did Vosoughi, Roy and Aral find about false news?
recall.a: It spread farther, faster and deeper than the truth, and people did most of the spreading.

recall.q: Name the four stages of virality.
recall.a: Seed, boost (a few high-reach accounts share it), cascade, saturate.

recall.q: Which stage is the best moment to intervene?
recall.a: The second stage, boost, when few nodes carry the claim and they are visible.

recall.q: Why are closed groups harder to counter?
recall.a: Nothing is visible to outsiders, nothing can be labelled, and the message arrives endorsed by someone trusted.

recall.q: Which classic sign of coordination has generative text weakened?
recall.a: Identical or near-identical wording across accounts.

sections.title: Echo Chambers & Filter Bubbles
sections.big_idea: A bubble is **done to you** by the ranking model; a chamber is **built by you.** Only the second is fully in your hands.
in_plain_words: Eli Pariser coined 'filter bubble' in 2011. Personalisation optimises predicted engagement and edits out the rest without telling you, so a feed presents itself as a window when it is a selection. An echo chamber is the social version, where you surround yourself with the like-minded. The two reinforce each other.

Homophily means networks were narrow before any algorithm touched them, and selective exposure is the demand that algorithms supply. The evidence on sealed bubbles is mixed: they are leaky, and matter most for highly engaged partisans. The real harm is relational. You stop meeting people who hold other views as people you could be wrong about.

right.title: Echo chamber
items: Partly visible: you know who you follow

diagram.caption: one is done to you, the other you help build

key_terms.meaning: Isolation caused by algorithms that show only what they predict you will like.
A social space of like-minded people where dissent is muffled.
The tendency to connect with people similar to ourselves.
Choosing sources that agree with your existing views.
Treating 'everyone I know thinks this' as a poll result.

worked_example.title: Bubble or chamber?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative cases. Decide which idea applies and what fix helps.
steps: Case 1: a feed stops showing a story you would have argued with, and you never learn it existed. The ranking model did this, so it is a filter bubble.
Case 2: you follow only people who share your views. Your choices did this, so it is an echo chamber.
Test case 1: open the same platform logged out in a private window and compare. The difference is the bubble.
Fixes: for the bubble, feed it different signals or use chronological or list views; for the chamber, add sources and people deliberately.
worked_example.answer: Case 1 is a filter bubble and case 2 is an echo chamber, and each has its own fix.

mistakes: Blaming algorithms for everything. Family, neighbourhood and language networks were narrow before any platform.
Assuming a balanced feed solves it. People still click what agrees, and the platform relearns within a week.
Following the other side's worst performers. It supplies evidence that they are ridiculous and feels like open-mindedness.
Treating the strong bubble story as settled. The evidence is mixed and the deck says so.

recall.q: Who coined 'filter bubble', and when?
recall.a: Eli Pariser, in 2011.

recall.q: Which of bubble and chamber is driven by your own choices?
recall.a: The echo chamber.

recall.q: What is homophily?
recall.a: The tendency to connect with people similar to ourselves.

recall.q: Name two harms of bubbles from the deck.
recall.a: Any two of: false consensus, loss of friction, norm shift, dehumanisation.

recall.q: Why does 'serious people you disagree with' matter?
recall.a: Following only the other side's worst performers supplies evidence that they are ridiculous.

sections.title: The Believing Brain
sections.big_idea: The mind's shortcuts were built for scarce information and known sources. **Read every slide here as being about you.**
in_plain_words: We find patterns fast, track who is in our group, trust the familiar and save effort. Each habit was useful once and each misfires online. Confirmation bias acts at search, interpretation, scrutiny and recall. Motivated reasoning asks 'can I believe this?' of welcome evidence and 'must I believe this?' of unwelcome evidence, and more numeracy can widen the partisan gap.

Repetition makes claims feel true through fluency, and a debunked claim lingers until a replacement explanation fills the gap it left. The backfire effect turned out to be rare, so correct. Dunning-Kruger is contested. The defence is a few specific habits, led by one question: would I check this if it cut the other way?

diagram.caption: six findings, all about how your own mind misfires

key_terms.meaning: Searching for, reading and recalling information so that it confirms what you believe.
Using reasoning to justify a conclusion you are emotionally committed to.
Repeating a statement raises the odds that people judge it true.
Misinformation keeps shaping reasoning even after a correction is accepted.
The ease with which something comes to mind, which does the work of repetition.

worked_example.title: Write a correction that fills the gap
worked_example.setup: A rumour says a vaccine causes infertility. Build the correction with the deck's own example.
steps: Weak version: 'The vaccine does not cause infertility.' It denies the claim and leaves a hole.
Ask where the rumour came from and why people believed it.
Fill the gap: 'The rumour began with a mistranslated study; the trials tracked pregnancies and found no difference.'
Lead with the truth and repeat the myth as little as you can, as section 11 advises.
worked_example.answer: A correction that supplies its own causal story, so the mind has something to use in place of the discredited account.

mistakes: Reading the section as being about other people. A reader thinking of a relative has missed the point.
Resolving to be open-minded afterwards. The counter is procedural: write down beforehand what would change your mind.
Skipping corrections because of the backfire effect. Later research found it rare, and clear correction usually helps.
Using Dunning-Kruger as an insult aimed outward. It is contested and the pattern includes the person citing it.

recall.q: At which four stages does confirmation bias act?
recall.a: Search, interpretation, scrutiny and recall.

recall.q: What does the illusory-truth effect say?
recall.a: Repeating a statement increases the likelihood that people judge it true.

recall.q: Why does a plain denial often fail?
recall.a: It leaves a hole where an explanation was, so the discredited account keeps being used.

recall.q: What happened to the backfire effect in later research?
recall.a: It was found to be rare and hard to reproduce.

recall.q: Which defence habit catches you when everything feels fine?
recall.a: Asking whether you would check this if it cut the other way.

sections.title: Propaganda & Manufacturing Consent
sections.big_idea: The aim has been constant for a century: **shape belief without seeming to.** Only the tooling gets cheaper and faster.
in_plain_words: Edward Bernays fused psychoanalysis with publicity and titled his 1928 book Propaganda. His method was to sell identity and feeling, and the product followed. Herman and Chomsky's 1988 propaganda model asks what shapes the news before anyone lies, and answers with five filters: ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak and a common enemy. The model is contested, and the question survives.

Framing and agenda-setting work without a single falsehood. A frame decides what you think about, and coverage choices decide which problems count. The firehose differs from classic propaganda. It floods the zone with contradictory claims and aims at cynicism, so refuting each claim feeds it. The response is to be the source that is consistently right.

diagram.caption: the five filters the news passes through

key_terms.meaning: Herman and Chomsky's claim that structural filters shape news without overt censorship.
Organised pushback that punishes inconvenient reporting.
Selecting and emphasising aspects of an issue to steer interpretation.
Media power over which issues the public thinks are important.
Many contradictory claims, fast, to exhaust and confuse instead of convince.

worked_example.title: Name the filter
worked_example.setup: Match each illustrative situation to one of the five filters.
steps: A newsroom with no budget for a reporter prints the ministry's press release. That is sourcing.
A publication is sued for defamation after an inconvenient story. That is flak.
Coverage treats scrutiny as disloyal because an external threat dominates debate. That is a common enemy.
An outlet owned by a conglomerate covers a sector where its owner has interests. That is ownership.
worked_example.answer: Sourcing, flak, a common enemy, ownership. Advertising is the fifth: outlets serve the audiences advertisers want.

mistakes: Reading the propaganda model as 'journalists are told what to write'. It describes structural tendencies and needs no plot.
Believing 'just report the facts' is possible. The choice of words is already an argument.
Rebutting a firehose claim by claim. The volume is the weapon and refutation feeds it.
Assuming good intentions separate persuasion from manipulation. You have to draw that line deliberately.

recall.q: Which book did Bernays publish in 1928?
recall.a: Propaganda.

recall.q: List the five filters.
recall.a: Ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak and a common enemy.

recall.q: Why do slow, large harms lose to fast, small ones for attention?
recall.a: Recurring harms stop being news and so stop being urgent.

recall.q: What does the firehose aim to produce?
recall.a: Cynicism: the belief that nothing is knowable.

recall.q: What has changed since 1928 in who can run a persuasion campaign?
recall.a: From corporations and states to anyone at all.

sections.title: The Attention Economy
sections.big_idea: Attention is scarce and content is abundant, so the feed rewards **engagement, and truth only when it happens to engage.**
in_plain_words: Platforms collect attention and data for free and sell predicted attention to advertisers. Revenue rewards whatever keeps you scrolling, and truth is outside the measurements. Whether a claim was true and the cost borne by the public sit outside the firm's boundary, which makes them externalities.

Nobody has to want the harm. A model learns that outrage predicts engagement and serves it, and creators then learn the gradient and drop the caveat. Design choices such as infinite scroll, variable rewards, streaks, notifications and autoplay remove decision points. The counter is friction, applied to yourself: restore the decision and pause before sharing what made you furious.

diagram.caption: truth was never the objective function

key_terms.meaning: An economy where human attention is the scarce resource bought and sold.
What the system is built to maximise; here, engagement.
A cost that falls outside the firm's boundary, such as damage to public truth.
The slot-machine schedule behind pull to refresh.
A restored decision point, such as autoplay off or a fixed slot.

worked_example.title: Match the design to the mechanism
worked_example.setup: For each feature, name the mechanism it borrows and a counter.
steps: Infinite scroll removes the stopping cue a page break used to supply.
Pull to refresh borrows variable reward, the slot-machine schedule.
Streaks use loss aversion, since quitting forfeits accumulated value.
Autoplay makes continuing the default, so stopping becomes the decision.
Counter for all: restore the decision point with autoplay and notifications off, and a fixed slot.
worked_example.answer: Each feature removes a decision, and friction puts it back.

mistakes: Looking only for a villain. The objective function does most of the harm, with nobody intending it.
Advising people to quit. Absolutist advice is rarely taken and unnecessary; the aim is to restore decision points.
Quoting the illustrative charts as data. Their heights are illustrative; the direction is the point.
Letting your own organisation strip the caveat from a finding to win attention. It spends its credibility.

recall.q: What did Herbert Simon say in 1971?
recall.a: A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.

recall.q: What is actually sold, according to the deck?
recall.a: Predicted attention, sliced by segment.

recall.q: Why is truth an externality?
recall.a: It is hard to measure and its cost falls on the public, outside the firm's boundary.

recall.q: Which practice is disproportionately effective?
recall.a: Pausing before sharing anything that angered you.

recall.q: What is the creator layer?
recall.a: Creators learn what the algorithm rewards and feed it, so the platform's incentive becomes theirs.

sections.title: Synthetic Media
sections.big_idea: Most harm today comes from **cheap edits to real media.** The deepest risk is that a recording stops proving anything.
in_plain_words: A photograph once proved something stood in front of a lens. Now it proves someone had software. The commonest damage still comes from cheapfakes: recaptioned, cropped, slowed or sped-up real media. The single commonest visual falsehood in South Asia is a real image with a false caption, beaten by a reverse image search.

Deepfakes are AI-made video, audio and images. The largest documented harm by volume is non-consensual intimate imagery, overwhelmingly of women. The liar's dividend is subtler: once fakes exist, the guilty can dismiss real evidence as AI. Generative text removes the language barrier, so teach provenance and habits, since no detector stays reliable for long.

right.title: AI-made
items: Voice clones from seconds of audio

diagram.caption: the left column does more damage today

key_terms.meaning: Misleading media made with simple edits or a false caption.
AI-generated video, audio or images of people doing or saying what they never did.
The guilty dismissing real evidence as fake, and being believed.
Who recorded it, where it came from and who vouches for the chain.
Searching an image to find where and when it first appeared.

worked_example.title: Diagnose four cases
worked_example.setup: Match each illustrative case to a form of synthetic or manipulated media and a check.
steps: An old riot photo recaptioned as today's local event. This is a miscontextualised image, a cheapfake. Reverse image search it.
A site with a name near a real outlet, registered weeks ago, no named editors. This is a fake outlet. Check the web address and look for an about page.
A phone call in a relative's voice asking for money. This is a voice clone used for fraud.
A thousand fluent local-language comments. This is generative scale, so look at behaviour and sources instead of the text.
worked_example.answer: Cheapfake, fake outlet, voice clone, generative scale. Three of the four are beaten by checking source and context.

mistakes: Training people to spot AI artefacts and not to reverse-search an image. It prepares them for the wrong threat.
Trusting last year's tells such as odd fingers or blinking. False confidence is worse than none.
Treating a recording as proof by default. Ask where it came from and who vouches for the chain.
Focusing on political deepfakes only. Non-consensual intimate imagery is the largest documented harm by volume.

recall.q: Which does more damage today, cheapfakes or deepfakes?
recall.a: Cheapfakes.

recall.q: What is the strongest single check for a fake news site?
recall.a: Search for the claim itself and see whether any other outlet reports it.

recall.q: What is the liar's dividend?
recall.a: Once people know any recording could be fake, the guilty can call real evidence a deepfake and be believed.

recall.q: Where was the Veles case, and what drove it?
recall.a: North Macedonia; teenagers chasing advertising revenue.

recall.q: Why should habits be taught ahead of detectors?
recall.a: No detector is reliable for long; source and context checks survive new models.

sections.title: Polarisation
sections.big_idea: The corrosive kind is **dislike of people**, which can grow while disagreement about policy shrinks.
in_plain_words: Ideological polarisation is real disagreement about policy and is healthy. Affective polarisation is dislike, distrust and fear of the other side as people. Its markers include not wanting your child to marry one of them, assuming the worst motive, and believing bad news about them without checking. That third marker makes disinformation land.

Humans form groups on arbitrary lines and favour their own, and caste, religion and language supply ready-made lines. Falsehood and division then feed each other in a loop, and trust in shared institutions falls until no referee remains. What reduces the heat: correct the caricature, build contact under equal and cooperative conditions, attack arguments and not identities, and refuse to share contempt.

diagram.caption: each turn makes the next falsehood easier to believe

key_terms.meaning: Disagreement about policy; normal and healthy.
Dislike and distrust of the other side as people.
Favouring your own group once any dividing line exists.
A task neither group can complete alone.
Falsehood and division feeding each other.

worked_example.title: Ideological or affective?
worked_example.setup: Label three illustrative statements, then pick an intervention.
steps: 'The tax rate should be lower.' This is a position on policy, so ideological.
'I would not want my child to marry one of them.' This is social distance, the classic affective marker.
'Whatever they do, they have a bad motive.' This assumes the worst motive by default, so affective.
If the problem is an exaggerated belief about how extreme the other side is, show the real distribution. It needs no one to change position.
worked_example.answer: Ideological, affective, affective. Correcting exaggerated beliefs is the cheapest intervention for the last two.

mistakes: Assuming that settling the policy disagreement ends the hostility. Affective polarisation can rise while positions converge.
Reading the markers as describing only the other side. They apply symmetrically.
Thinking 'bring them together' is a plan. Unequal, competitive or supervised-from-above contact can harden hostility.
Treating the trust chart as national data. It is an illustrative downward trend.

recall.q: Which kind of polarisation is corrosive?
recall.a: Affective polarisation.

recall.q: How does the deck measure it?
recall.a: Feeling thermometers, willingness to marry, and trust.

recall.q: What did minimal-group experiments show?
recall.a: A coin toss was enough to produce in-group favouritism.

recall.q: Which intervention is cheapest and least known?
recall.a: Correcting exaggerated beliefs about how extreme the other side is.

recall.q: Why does a superordinate goal work better than dialogue sessions?
recall.a: Joint work on a task neither group can complete alone reduces favouritism faster than contact alone.

sections.title: Why It Matters for Development
sections.big_idea: Falsehood is an **operational risk** to every programme that relies on public trust, and belongs on the risk list.
in_plain_words: Frame post-truth as a media-studies concern and it loses to every operational priority. Frame it as a risk to uptake, staff safety and community trust and it earns a budget. Rumours stall immunisation, suppress ID enrolment, withdraw girls from school and undo sanitation uptake. A concrete ask is rumour monitoring in your feedback channels and one named person who can respond within a day.

Several patterns repeat. Vaccine fertility rumours draw force from real memories of coercion. Forwards about child-kidnappers, cattle or blasphemy have led to lynchings. Communal disinformation redirects a real grievance onto a group. Election falsehood is timed so correction cannot finish, and manufactured doubt delays action on science. The deepest cost is eroded trust, which collective action needs.

diagram.caption: where a falsehood costs a programme

key_terms.meaning: A threat to uptake, staff safety or community trust, to be logged and owned.
Watching community feedback channels for rumours, with a named responder.
A real grievance redirected onto a group that did not cause it.
Exaggerating uncertainty to delay action, without outright denial.
Cooperation that depends on shared facts and trusted referees.

worked_example.title: Put a rumour on the risk list
worked_example.setup: An illustrative girls' education programme hears claims about safety and conversion.
steps: Name the programme area: girls' education. The table says such claims withdraw girls from school.
Add rumour monitoring to the community feedback channels you already run.
Name one person who can respond within a day.
Answer in the language and channel of the rumour, using trusted local voices, and be present before the next rumour.
Treat staff safety as a risk from the first day, before any incident.
worked_example.answer: A logged risk, a named responder, a monitored channel, a local-language reply, and a staff-safety plan.

mistakes: Treating post-truth as a media-studies curiosity. Framed as a risk to uptake and safety, it gets funded.
Calling a fertility rumour stupid. It argues with a real memory of coercion and loses.
Preparing for an election after a claim appears. Timing is the design, so responses must be pre-built.
Dismissing the grievance behind communal disinformation. That hands the field to whoever will address it.

recall.q: Why does a rumour about a health campaign need a staff-safety response?
recall.a: Health workers, including polio workers, have been attacked and killed over rumours.

recall.q: Name the four steps of the communal disinformation pattern.
recall.a: A real grievance or fear, a false or miscontextualised incident, a named group as the cause, repetition.

recall.q: Which election tactic does the most durable damage?
recall.a: Pre-emptive claims of rigging, which teach a public that counting cannot be trusted.

recall.q: What does 'doubt is our product' refer to?
recall.a: A tobacco memo whose strategy was reused against climate science.

recall.q: What does collective action need that erosion removes?
recall.a: A shared account of facts, a trusted referee, belief that others will comply, and willingness to bear a cost now.

sections.title: Building Resilience
sections.big_idea: You will not catch every lie, so aim to make people **harder to fool, quicker to check and slower to spread.**
in_plain_words: Delete, debunk and detect are supply-side goals that lose on cost or speed. Resilience is demand-side and generalises to lies nobody has written yet. Fact-checking is a public good with limits: it is slower than falsehood and rarely reaches closed groups. Lateral reading, which means leaving the page to see what others say about it, is the highest-yield habit.

Prebunking teaches a technique before the lie arrives, with modest effects that fade and need boosters. If you must debunk, use the truth sandwich and repeat the myth once. Media and information literacy compounds over a lifetime if it teaches calibrated trust. The citizen's checklist compresses everything: pause, check the source, date and place, cross-check, reverse-search, and if unsure do not forward.

key_terms.meaning: People and communities harder to fool, quicker to check and slower to spread.
Leaving a page to check what other sources say about it.
Forewarning about a manipulation technique before people meet it.
Truth, then a brief myth, then truth again.
Media and information literacy: sourcing, verifying, contextualising, questioning.

worked_example.title: Write a truth sandwich
worked_example.setup: A video of a violent scene is circulating as a local incident. Use the deck's wording for a correction.
steps: Open with the truth as the headline: this video was filmed in another country in 2019, and here is the original.
Warn briefly: a false claim is circulating that it shows a local event.
Repeat the myth once, briefly, and keep it out of the headline and the image.
Explain why it is wrong and who benefits if people believe it.
Replace the gap with the true account, then close by restating the truth.
worked_example.answer: A correction whose most memorable sentence is the truth. Test it: if someone read only the headline and image, what would they believe?

mistakes: Judging a site by its design and tone. Professional appearance is the cheapest thing to fake.
Putting the myth in the headline or image of a correction. People remember the vivid claim.
Teaching media literacy as blanket suspicion. The aim is calibrated trust, including recognising reliable sources.
Treating prebunking as a cure. Effects fade over weeks and it does not protect against a determined campaign.

recall.q: Why is resilience the better goal than detection?
recall.a: It generalises to new falsehoods, while detection is an arms race against models that improve monthly.

recall.q: What did the lateral reading study compare?
recall.a: Historians, undergraduates and fact-checkers; fact-checkers did best by opening new tabs.

recall.q: Who traced inoculation theory, and who revived it?
recall.a: William McGuire in the 1960s, revived by Sander van der Linden and colleagues.

recall.q: List the five MIL questions.
recall.a: Who made this and what do they gain, what is the evidence, what is missing, how does it want me to feel, what does it want me to do.

recall.q: Which checklist step works even when you cannot tell?
recall.a: If unsure, do not forward.

notes.2: This agenda is a **map of eleven sections**, each with its slide range so you can jump. Slide 10 later suggests a short route if time is tight, and a different start for programme managers. Skim the list now and note which section answers your job's question.
notes.4: Fix the sense of the word first. **'Post' means facts no longer settle the argument**, and it does not mean they have vanished. Then keep the objection in view: elites manipulated publics long before 2016, so the deck argues that the infrastructure is new and the impulse is old.
notes.5: Use the second row of the table as your test. **Lying is old; what changes a system is whether being caught costs anything.** When a falsehood signals loyalty, exposure can raise standing. The practical aim is to rebuild a referee both sides trust, by being right when it is inconvenient.
notes.6: Read the right-hand column of the cost table as the argument of the whole course. Each barrier to a falsehood was a cost, and each has fallen to roughly nothing. **Production got free and verification did not.** A response built on out-producing falsehood is arguing against arithmetic.
notes.7: Four symptoms, and none needs a liar. That is why the diagnosis helps: ordinary commercial and technological pressure is enough. Try the cheapest fix first. **Mark opinion as opinion, visibly**, including in your own organisation's communication, which blurs the line as often as any platform does.
notes.8: Five conditions stack up here: phones, closed chats, many languages, kinship networks and existing fault lines. The row to remember is the fourth. **A forward carries the credibility of the person who sent it**, and in a family group there is no visible post for anyone to label.
notes.9: A scope slide that doubles as a warning about your own temptations. Each comfortable answer in the table fails for a stated reason. **Resilience is slower and less satisfying than a fix**, and it needs nobody to win an argument. In a training room, never let half the audience feel superior.
notes.10: Use the roadmap table to find the section that answers your question. The course splits into diagnosis and response. With limited time, read sections 2, 5 and 11, which **change behaviour**, and leave the rest as the explanation of why the behaviour is needed.
notes.12: Before you call anything fake news, ask two questions: **is it false, and was harm intended?** The answers sort the field into three categories. The phrase itself has become an insult for reporting someone dislikes, which is why researchers use the sharper words on the next slides.
notes.13: Learn the table as two axes: falseness and intent to harm. **The category depends on who sent the message and when**, so the same words are misinformation in an aunt's hands and disinformation in a seller's. You cannot classify a message by reading it alone.
notes.14: Misinformation is sincere, and sincerity is why it travels. When a relative forwards something false, use the left column: **correct in private, credit the motive, give a replacement fact, show the check.** The last habit compounds, because one person who can reverse-search an image becomes a check for the whole group.
notes.15: Engineered falsehood leaves marks: timing, identical wording, a fault-line target, polish and a beneficiary. Start with **'who gains if this is believed, or merely doubted?'** It is a prompt to check and never proof. Used carelessly it produces conspiracy theory, since a beneficiary can be found for any claim.
notes.16: Malinformation passes every fact-check because each claim is true. The deception sits in selection, framing and timing, so **a checker working claim by claim will rate it true.** Telling it from accountability journalism comes down to public interest, which you have to argue because no tool can detect it.
notes.17: Six forms, each with its own fuel. Read the first row for action: rumour fills an information vacuum, so **say something true and specific early**, even if it is only what you know and when you will know more. The last row explains why arguing with a conspiracy theory rarely works.
notes.18: Context collapse is the general mechanism and satire is its clearest case. A screenshot loses the publication name, the surrounding page and the audience that knew the format. **Restore the frame**: link the original, name the publication, show the crop. Taking the piece down only creates a grievance.
notes.19: Keep this slide open when you respond. Match the label to the action: **educate, debunk or defend.** The commonest error is treating a worried relative as an operation. The second is patiently fact-checking a coordinated campaign claim by claim, which is exactly what the campaign is built to absorb.
notes.21: Use the misattributed quote as your worked example. A tidy line outran a messier history, among people who worry about attribution, and nobody lied. Take away one habit: **when a quotation is unusually well phrased for your point, check it before you use it.**
notes.22: The chart is illustrative but the study is real, covering about 126,000 stories on Twitter. False news spread farther, faster and deeper, and **people did most of the spreading**. Cite it with its limits: one platform, one period, stories rated by fact-checking organisations.
notes.23: Two findings explain the gap. False stories were more novel, and they set off surprise and disgust where true ones set off sadness and trust. **Humans did most of the spreading**, so removing bots would not close it. An intervention aimed only at bots is aimed at the smaller half.
notes.24: Learn four stages in order: seed, boost, cascade, saturate. The best moment to intervene is the second, when few nodes carry the claim and they are visible. Most institutions respond at stage four. **'I keep seeing it' tells you about the network's shape and nothing about the claim.**
notes.25: Read the chart as repeated multiplication. Each person forwards to several others, so reach grows with every hop, and hubs such as large groups speed it up. In South Asia a forward from a relative carries the relationship's credibility. **The receiver trusts the sender and rarely asks about the source.**
notes.26: Compare the open and closed columns. A closed group has no like-count, no label and no visible origin, and the message arrives endorsed by someone you trust. **The interventions that work here are social**: forward limits to slow velocity, and one liked, competent person inside the group who checks things.
notes.27: Bots boost; they rarely persuade. Their real target is your estimate of what everyone thinks, and **social proof does the rest** as real people adopt a view that looks widely held. Be careful with the accusation, which is often used to dismiss a person. Ask for evidence of coordination.
notes.28: CIB is defined by behaviour: deception about who is speaking. Look for bursts of timing, accounts created together and shared infrastructure. The first row concedes something useful. **Copy-pasted wording is no longer a reliable tell**, because generative tools write a thousand distinct posts. Detection is moving to behaviour.
notes.30: Pariser's worry is that personalisation edits your information invisibly. Read the last row closely: **a feed presents itself as a window when it is a selection.** Test it by opening the same platform logged out in a private window. The difference between the two is your bubble.
notes.31: Keep the two ideas apart because the fixes differ. A bubble is done to you by the ranking model; an echo chamber is built by your own choices. **Only one is under your control**, and auditing who you follow needs no platform's permission. They compound because each feeds the other.
notes.32: This single picture is the whole mechanism: everything goes in and only what the model predicts you will engage with comes out. The key word is silently. **You never see what was dropped**, so nothing inside the feed tells you a filter exists.
notes.33: Homophily limits how far you can blame algorithms. Family, neighbourhood, language and workplace networks were narrow before any platform. Use the fourth row: **mixed workplaces, classrooms and programme groups** are where cross-group contact happens, so contact is a development recommendation as well as a media one.
notes.34: Selective exposure is the demand and the filter bubble is the supply. That is why supply-side fixes disappoint: given a balanced feed, people click what agrees and the platform rebuilds the imbalance within a week. **Reading the other side only through mockery counts as reinforcement.**
notes.35: A balanced course has to say this: the evidence on sealed bubbles is mixed. Average diets are more varied than the strong story suggests, and incidental exposure still happens. **Meeting the other side is a different thing from being open to it**, and hostile exposure can raise hostility.
notes.36: Four harms: false consensus, lost friction, norm shift and dehumanisation. The damage that matters most is relational. For your own team, take the second row: **a team where nobody disagrees is unchecked and only looks aligned.** Appoint someone whose job is to argue the other case.
notes.37: Treat these four as practice you repeat. The load-bearing phrase is 'serious people you disagree with'. Following the other side's worst performers feeds you evidence that they are ridiculous. **Every click trains the model**, so a deliberate week changes your feed, and it reverts within days.
notes.39: Read this whole section as being about you. The mind's habits (finding patterns, tracking the tribe, trusting the familiar, saving effort) suited a world of scarce information and known sources. They misfire in an environment built by people who studied them. **A reader thinking of a relative has missed the value.**
notes.40: Confirmation bias acts at four points: search, interpretation, scrutiny and recall. The third bites professionals hardest, because uneven scrutiny feels exactly like rigour. The counter is procedural: **decide what evidence would change your mind before you look, and write it down.** Resolving to be open-minded afterwards does little.
notes.41: Motivated reasoning asks 'can I believe this?' of welcome evidence and 'must I believe this?' of unwelcome evidence. More numeracy can widen the partisan gap. The check that sometimes works is to **swap the sides** and ask what you would conclude. Adding facts alone is a weak design for identity-linked issues.
notes.42: Repetition makes a statement feel true even when you know better. The mechanism is fluency, the ease with which a thing comes to mind. Notice the group chat row: **four relatives forwarding one message read as four sources.** Debunking also rehearses the myth, which leads to the rule in section 11.
notes.43: This is the deck's best self-referential example. A striking finding, that correction backfires, travelled faster than its own correction among people whose job is correcting. **Later research found backfire rare and hard to reproduce**, so for most people a clear correction helps. Do not let the myth stop you.
notes.44: A denial leaves a hole where an explanation was, and the mind keeps using the discredited account until something replaces it. Compare the columns: each strong correction tells a causal story. **Answer 'where did this come from and why did people believe it?'** along with 'it is false'.
notes.45: Handle this finding with care. In its popular form, 'stupid people think they are geniuses', it is contested, and part of the pattern is a statistical artefact. The sturdier point needs no contested effect: **confident, unhedged claims travel better than careful ones**, and experts arrive hedged. That is a communication problem.
notes.46: Five habits, each tied to a moment. A few specific rules fire at the right time, while a long list of biases does not. If you adopt one, adopt the first: **would I check this if it cut the other way?** It catches you when everything feels fine, which is when the error happens.
notes.48: Bernays used 'propaganda' as a neutral professional word and defended manipulation openly. The candour is the striking part, and the techniques outlived the word. If you run campaigns, including health ones, **draw the line between persuasion and manipulation deliberately**, because good intentions do not draw it for you.
notes.49: Move from the left to the right column: selling a feature, then selling an identity. The right column is harder to argue with because a counter-argument threatens who the listener is. For programmes this means **messaging that contradicts a held identity loses**, however good the evidence behind it.
notes.50: Read the model's claim and its common misreading side by side. It describes structural filters and systematic tendencies. It needs no conspiracy and explains no single article. It was built for a broadcast era, so today's filter is a ranking model. **Keep its question**: what shapes the news before anyone lies?
notes.51: Learn the five filters as a list: ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, a common enemy. The quiet one is sourcing. A newsroom that cannot afford a reporter runs the press release, and **coverage is shaped with no one applying pressure**. Apply all five to reporting in your own sector.
notes.52: No unframed way to describe a contested thing exists, so 'just report the facts' is unavailable as an instruction. Every row of the table is defensible and none is neutral. The last row is ours: **'beneficiary' became 'rights holder'** through deliberate reframing by practitioners. We use this mechanism too.
notes.53: Agenda-setting works through choices about coverage and prominence. The fourth row hurts development most: recurring harms stop being news and so stop being urgent, which is why slow, large harms lose to fast, small ones. **To get a chronic problem covered, supply a date, a changed number or a person who will speak.**
notes.54: The firehose floods the zone with contradictory claims to produce cynicism. Compare the columns: consistency is irrelevant and refutation feeds it, so checking claim by claim loses. What remains is **being the source that is consistently, boringly right**, and explaining the technique instead of each instance.
notes.55: Read the last column of the table, who could run a persuasion campaign. It moves from corporations and states to anyone at all. The aim stayed the same for a century and only the tooling got cheaper. **Institutions built to check influence were designed for the first two rows**, which is why regulation lags.
notes.57: Start from scarcity: attention is scarce and content is abundant. Herbert Simon's 1971 point is that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. The adage 'you are the product' is neat but imprecise. **What is sold is predicted attention, sliced by segment.**
notes.58: Truth was never the objective function; engagement is. The right-hand column lists what the system cannot measure, including whether a claim was true. These are externalities, costs that fall on the public. Ask what would make the cost land inside the firm's boundary, because **every serious regulatory proposal answers that question**.
notes.59: The chart is illustrative, so read its shape and ignore exact heights. Content that triggers moral outrage tends to be shared most, so an engagement-chasing algorithm learns to serve anger. **Nobody has to decide this.** It follows from the objective the system was given.
notes.60: Another illustrative chart: the share of adults who get news mainly through social media and messaging. Magnitudes are not exact, so use the direction only. When the feed is the front page, **the engagement algorithm acts as the editor**, and it is tuned for attention.
notes.61: Each design choice borrows a mechanism: infinite scroll removes the stopping cue, pull to refresh uses variable reward, streaks use loss aversion, autoplay makes continuing the default. All were built to hold attention. The cheap counter has one shape: **restore the missing decision point.** Friction is the whole intervention.
notes.62: This is the most important slide in the section and it persuades least, because it removes the villain. A model learned that outrage predicts engagement, and nobody chose the result. **Fix the objective or who bears the cost.** Responsibility remains, since choosing and keeping the objective are human decisions.
notes.63: The incentive flows downhill from platform to creator to public. No falsehood is needed at any step: a careful person who wants an audience follows the gradient into overconfident content. It reaches institutions too, as **pressure to strip the caveat from a finding** spends their credibility. Keep your caveats.
notes.64: Four practices, and none of them is quitting. Start with the cheapest: notifications off except people, autoplay off. The last row matters most. **Pause before sharing anything that angered you**, because anger most reliably turns a reader into a spreader. The aim is to restore the decision points the design removed.
notes.66: Treat this as a ladder of what a photograph proved. Film needed a darkroom; now an image proves someone had software. The loss is of a default, because 'there is footage' used to end arguments. What replaces it is **provenance**, which is slower. Keep proportion, since cheap manipulation does most damage today.
notes.67: A fake outlet needs no AI. Run the five checks in seconds and favour the fourth: **search for the claim itself, outside the site.** People skip it because it means leaving the page, which is the lateral-reading habit in section 11. The Veles teenagers had no politics, only advertising revenue.
notes.68: Cheapfakes are simple edits to real media: recaptioning, cropping, slowing or speeding. They have done far more damage than deepfakes, yet deepfakes draw the coverage and funding. **Provenance checking works on all four rows**; artefact-spotting works on only the last, and will not for long.
notes.69: This is the commonest visual falsehood in the region and the easiest to beat. A real image recaptioned as local needs no technology. Teach the action itself: **long-press an image and search it, on the person's own phone**. 'Check images' as a principle changes nothing. Also ask who wants you angry, and at whom.
notes.70: Deepfakes are AI-made video, audio or images of people saying or doing things they never did. Take the third row seriously: non-consensual intimate imagery, overwhelmingly of women, used to silence and extort. **Assume the capability exists**, since a voice clone needs only seconds of audio.
notes.71: The liar's dividend is the more serious half of the deepfake problem. Once fakes exist, the guilty can wave away real evidence as AI, and **denial needs only the existence of the technology.** The burden shifts to whoever holds the recording. It falls unevenly, because the powerful have lawyers and the benefit of the doubt.
notes.72: Generative AI removed the old limits on disinformation: convincing writing, volume, images and sounding local. For smaller South Asian languages the first row matters most, since fluent falsehood once needed a fluent person. Shift effort **from detecting content to provenance, source reputation and behavioural signals.**
notes.73: Habits beat detectors. The durable skills concern context: check the source and chain, reverse-search, ask whether a credible outlet reports it, distrust emotionally perfect clips. **Do not teach artefact-spotting as the main skill.** Last year's tells are already gone, and false confidence is worse than none.
notes.75: Polarisation comes in two kinds. Ideological disagreement about policy is healthy. Affective polarisation is dislike and distrust of people, and it can grow **while policy positions converge.** For programmes this matters: reducing disagreement may leave hostility alone, and hostility decides whether two communities can share a water committee.
notes.76: Use the four markers as a self-test and apply them to your own side first. The third explains why this section sits in a course on falsehood: **a claim about a disliked group needs almost no evidence**, because the audience has already decided the group is capable of it.
notes.77: Group favouritism appears on arbitrary lines, even a coin toss, and caste, religion and language carry far more material. Disinformation finds a fault line and pours in water. The actionable row is the last: **a shared goal that needs both groups** reduces favouritism faster than contact alone.
notes.78: Read the loop clockwise: a falsehood about them produces anger and distrust, which deepens division, which makes the next falsehood easier to believe. Division is both cause and product. Because the loop feeds itself, interrupt it at the earliest step you can reach, and the next slides list options.
notes.79: The chart shows an illustrative downward trend, so read the direction and not the figures. The point is structural: when no source is trusted in common, **there is no shared referee**, each side keeps its own facts, and the condition sustains itself. Link this back to the referee question on slide 5.
notes.80: Four interventions with different strengths of evidence. The cheapest and least known is the first: people overestimate how extreme the other side is, and **showing the real distribution moves hostility** without anyone changing position. Contact helps only under equal, cooperative conditions. The conditions are the intervention.
notes.82: This is the slide that gets the budget. Frame post-truth as a risk to uptake, staff safety and community trust, and it lands on the risk list. The ask is concrete: **add rumour monitoring to your feedback channels and name a person** who can respond within a day. The second is what most organisations lack.
notes.83: Look at the second row. Fertility rumours about vaccines have drawn force from real memories of coercive family planning, so a campaign that calls the belief stupid is arguing with a memory. **Trust cannot be built during a crisis.** Treat hostile rumours as a staff-safety issue from the first day.
notes.84: These tragedies share one shape: a stranger, an unverifiable warning and a crowd that acts before any authority arrives. Technology supplies the speed and a plausible image. The slide lists what has helped: **forward limits, a verified police account within hours, and local volunteers** who can say where a photograph is from.
notes.85: Learn the four-step pattern: a real grievance, a false incident, a named group, repetition. Seeing the shape assemble is quicker than checking each claim. The first row is usually authentic, so **communal disinformation redirects a real grievance** onto a group that did not cause it. Dismissing the grievance hands the field to others.
notes.86: Each tactic is placed where the correction cycle cannot finish, so election responses must be **pre-built**: verified channels, a named spokesperson, prepared material. The fourth row does the most lasting damage, because a public taught in advance that counting cannot be trusted carries that belief into every later election.
notes.87: The doubt playbook never needs a lie: fund marginal research, demand impossible certainty, promote a few dissenters, attack the messenger, insist on balance. The last row implicates journalism. **Balance is a virtue between contested positions** and a distortion between a settled finding and a paid dissenter. You must judge which case you face.
notes.88: The deepest cost is that cooperation becomes almost impossible. Development is collective action, and each row shows what it needs and what erosion removes. Rebuilding is slow and local: institutions that are accurate when it costs them, over years. **There is no campaign for trust**, which is why the next section aims at resilience.
notes.90: State the goal carefully. Delete, debunk and detect are supply-side and lose on cost or speed. Making people harder to fool is demand-side, and only that **scales to lies nobody has written yet.** It is also the slowest, and it loses funding contests to detection tools that demo well.
notes.91: Fact-checking deserves defence as a public good, and this slide is about its limits. It builds a citable record and raises costs for public figures. It cannot reach closed groups, disposable accounts or the speed gap. **A correction is only as persuasive as the corrector is trusted**, and exposed audiences are often taught to distrust checkers.
notes.92: Lateral reading is probably the highest-yield technique in the deck. Leave the page and search what others say about it. In the comparison study, fact-checkers reached better judgements in less time **simply by opening new tabs.** Professional appearance is the cheapest thing on a website to fake; reputation is not.
notes.93: Prebunking teaches the technique before the lie arrives, so it covers claims not yet invented. The results are consistent and modest: effects decay over weeks and need boosters, like a vaccine. **Do not oversell it.** It gives no protection against a determined campaign aimed at an identity someone holds.
notes.94: Memorise three beats: warn, expose a weakened example, refute by showing the trick. The picture works because it teaches the technique, such as fake experts or emotional manipulation. That makes the resistance reach lies you have never seen and **last longer than debunking one claim at a time**.
notes.95: Walk the six steps in order and test your draft against the third: repeat the myth once, briefly, never in the headline or image. Then ask the check question: **if someone read only the headline and the image, what would they believe?** That is what most of your audience will do.
notes.96: Media literacy is the long game because it compounds. The five questions work at fourteen and at forty. One caution from the field: taught badly, it produces blanket cynicism. **Aim for calibrated trust**, which means teaching people to recognise a reliable source as well as an unreliable one.
notes.97: Treat this as a card for the moment of decision, since each check takes seconds to a minute. The last row matters most: **if unsure, do not forward.** It costs nothing, needs no skill, and removes one node from the cascade. It is the only step that works even when you cannot tell.
notes.98: If you read one source, read the 2018 Science paper. Knowing it covers one platform, one period and fact-checker-rated stories lets you cite it accurately while others round it up. Pair the deck with the three ImpactMojo courses it names: Data Literacy, Media & Communications, and Digital Rights & AI 101.
notes.99: Five takeaways, then five actions: pause before forwarding, reverse-search images, read laterally, name what would change your mind, correct relatives in private. All need no budget. Remember the balance in the last row: **habits do not fix an incentive structure**, and both halves are true.
